title: Biomolecules: Carbohydrates, Lipids, Proteins, Enzymes and Minerals

toc.title: 1.1 Carbohydrates and lipids: structure, types and biological role
1.3 Proteins and enzymes: structure, types and biological role

html:
Basic Components of Life is the first unit of the Botany section and carries 2 of the 40 Botany questions.

Both are almost always straight recall or one-step reasoning: which bond joins the glucose units of cellulose, which sugar is non-reducing, which mineral sits in chlorophyll or in nitrogenase, what a competitive inhibitor does to K_m, which class an enzyme belongs to.

The chapter is short to read and quick to score — every fact below has been asked in some form by entrance setters, so learn the tables.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Carbohydrate classes — mono-, di- and polysaccharides; aldose or ketose; reducing or non-reducing (sucrose is the non-reducing one).
  • Glycosidic bonds — α-1,4 (starch, glycogen), α-1,6 (their branch points), β-1,4 (cellulose, chitin); inulin is a fructose polymer.
  • Lipids — triglyceride = glycerol + 3 fatty acids (ester bonds, 3 H₂O lost); saturated vs unsaturated; phospholipids, steroids, waxes.
  • Mineral roles and deficiency signs — Mg in chlorophyll, Mo in nitrogenase, Mn and Cl in water splitting, Ca in the middle lamella; mobile elements show symptoms in old leaves first.
  • Protein structure — peptide bond, four levels and the bonds that hold each, fibrous vs globular, simple vs conjugated.
  • Enzymes — cofactors, lock-and-key vs induced fit, K_m, the effect of temperature, pH and inhibitors, and the six IUB classes with one example each.

1.1 Carbohydrates and lipids: structure, types and biological role

Carbohydrates

Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or substances that give these on hydrolysis.

Most fit the formula Cₙ(H₂O)ₙ — "hydrates of carbon" — but the formula is only a guide: deoxyribose (C₅H₁₀O₄) is a carbohydrate that does not fit it, and acetic acid (C₂H₄O₂) fits it but is not a carbohydrate.

A sugar with a free aldehyde group (–CHO) is an aldose; one with a ketone group (>C=O) is a ketose.

Class Number of carbons Aldose example Ketose example Where it matters
Triose 3 glyceraldehyde (PGAL) dihydroxyacetone (DHAP) first sugars of the Calvin cycle and glycolysis
Tetrose 4 erythrose erythrulose erythrose-4-phosphate in the Calvin cycle
Pentose 5 ribose, deoxyribose, xylose ribulose RNA, DNA; RuBP is the CO₂ acceptor
Hexose 6 glucose, galactose, mannose fructose respiratory fuel; fruit sugar
Heptose 7 glucoheptose sedoheptulose Calvin cycle

Glucose (dextrose, grape sugar) is an aldohexose; fructose (laevulose, fruit sugar) is a ketohexose and the sweetest natural sugar. In water, hexoses close into rings.

In α-glucose the –OH on carbon 1 lies below the plane of the ring; in β-glucose it lies above. That single difference decides whether the polymer is a digestible fuel (starch, α) or an indigestible fibre (cellulose, β).

Two sugars join by a glycosidic bond, formed by condensation (loss of one H₂O) and broken by hydrolysis. Oligosaccharides have 2–10 sugar units.

Disaccharide Units Bond Reducing? Source / role
Sucrose glucose + fructose α-1 → β-2 No cane, beet; the transport sugar of the phloem
Maltose glucose + glucose α-1,4 Yes germinating barley (malt); starch digestion
Lactose galactose + glucose β-1,4 Yes milk sugar
Cellobiose glucose + glucose β-1,4 Yes breakdown product of cellulose
Trehalose glucose + glucose α-1,1 No fungi; the blood sugar of insects

Sucrose is non-reducing because the bond joins the reducing carbons of both units (C-1 of glucose and C-2 of fructose), so no free carbonyl group is left.

Its hydrolysis by invertase (sucrase) gives an equal mixture of glucose and fructose called invert sugar — the optical rotation changes from dextro to laevo, hence the name.

Raffinose (galactose + glucose + fructose) is a common non-reducing trisaccharide of seeds.

Polysaccharides (glycans) are long chains of hundreds to thousands of units. They are insoluble, non-sweet and non-reducing, which is exactly why they make good stores.

Polysaccharide Monomer Bonds Shape Iodine colour Role and occurrence
Amylose (≈20–25 % of starch) α-glucose α-1,4 unbranched helix blue-black plant food store
Amylopectin (≈75–80 % of starch) α-glucose α-1,4 + α-1,6 branches every ~24–30 units branched red-violet plant food store
Glycogen α-glucose α-1,4 + α-1,6 branches every ~8–12 units highly branched red-brown store of animals and fungi ("animal starch")
Cellulose β-glucose β-1,4 straight chains in microfibrils none plant cell wall; the most abundant organic compound on Earth
Chitin N-acetylglucosamine β-1,4 straight none fungal cell wall, insect exoskeleton
Inulin fructose β-2,1 short chains none stored in the tuberous roots of Dahlia and dandelion
Pectin galacturonic acid α-1,4 — none middle lamella (as calcium pectate)
Peptidoglycan (murein) NAG + NAM with short peptides β-1,4 + peptide cross-links net-like sac none bacterial cell wall
Agar, carrageenan galactose (partly sulphated) — — none red algae (Gelidium, Gracilaria)
Three favourite traps
  1. Sucrose is non-reducing; maltose and lactose are reducing. "All disaccharides reduce Benedict's solution" is false.
  2. Inulin is a fructose polymer, not glucose — and glycogen, not starch, is the store of fungi.
  3. Cellulose and starch are both glucose. They differ only in α versus β linkage, and humans lack the enzyme (cellulase) that splits the β-1,4 bond between glucose units; cattle digest grass only with the help of cellulase-making microbes in the rumen.
Test Reagent Positive result Detects
Molisch's α-naphthol + conc. H₂SO₄ violet ring at the junction any carbohydrate
Benedict's / Fehling's alkaline Cu²⁺ (Benedict's: CuSO₄, sodium citrate, Na₂CO₃) brick-red Cu₂O on boiling reducing sugars
Barfoed's copper acetate in acetic acid red precipitate within ~2 min monosaccharides (disaccharides react slowly)
Seliwanoff's resorcinol + HCl quick cherry-red ketoses (fructose)
Iodine I₂ in KI blue-black starch (amylose)

Biological roles. Carbohydrates are the main respiratory fuel (glucose gives about 17 kJ g⁻¹); storage (starch, glycogen, inulin); structure (cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin, chitin, peptidoglycan); the sugar part of nucleotides (ribose, deoxyribose) and of ATP, NAD, FAD and coenzyme A; and recognition markers on cell surfaces (glycoproteins and glycolipids, including the ABO blood-group antigens).

Agar from red algae solidifies microbiological culture media.

Lipids

Lipids are esters of fatty acids with alcohols (or substances related to them) that are insoluble in water and soluble in organic solvents such as ether, chloroform and benzene.

Unlike carbohydrates and proteins, they are not polymers — a triglyceride is a small molecule (relative molecular mass usually below 1000) built from four parts, not a chain of repeating units.

Type What it is Examples
Simple lipids — fats and oils ester of glycerol + 3 fatty acids (triglyceride) ghee, butter, mustard oil
Simple lipids — waxes ester of a long-chain fatty acid + a long-chain monohydric alcohol cuticle wax, beeswax, lanolin
Compound lipids — phospholipids glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate + a base lecithin (choline), cephalin (ethanolamine)
Compound lipids — others lipid + sugar or protein glycolipids (cerebrosides), lipoproteins
Derived lipids — steroids four fused rings (three 6-carbon + one 5-carbon) cholesterol (animals), ergosterol (fungi), sitosterol (plants), sex hormones, brassinosteroids
Derived lipids — terpenes built from isoprene (C₅H₈) units carotenoids, rubber, essential oils (menthol), phytol tail of chlorophyll, gibberellins

A triglyceride forms when each of the three –OH groups of glycerol makes an ester bond with the –COOH of a fatty acid; three molecules of water are released. A fatty acid is a hydrocarbon chain (usually 14–20 carbons, almost always an even number) ending in –COOH.

Feature Saturated fatty acid Unsaturated fatty acid
C=C double bonds none one (mono-) or more (poly-unsaturated)
Chain shape straight, packs tightly kinked at each cis double bond
State of its fat at room temperature solid (fat) liquid (oil)
Examples palmitic (C16:0), stearic (C18:0) oleic (C18:1), linoleic (C18:2), linolenic (C18:3), arachidonic (C20:4)
Typical source ghee, butter, coconut and palm oil mustard, sunflower, soybean, fish oil

Essential fatty acids — linoleic and linolenic acid (arachidonic acid is made from linoleic) — cannot be made by animals and must come from plant food.

Hydrogenating an oil with a nickel catalyst saturates its double bonds and turns it into a solid cooking fat (vanaspati ghee).

A phospholipid is amphipathic: its phosphate head is hydrophilic and its two fatty-acid tails are hydrophobic, so in water phospholipids line up tail-to-tail into the bilayer of every cell membrane.

Cutin (in the cuticle) and suberin (in cork and the Casparian strip) are lipid polymers that waterproof plant surfaces.

Why seeds store oil

Lipids give about 39 kJ g⁻¹ (9.3 kcal g⁻¹) on oxidation against about 17 kJ g⁻¹ (4.1 kcal g⁻¹) for carbohydrate and protein — more than twice as much — because their carbon is far less oxidised, and they are stored without water.

Mustard, groundnut, sesame and sunflower seeds therefore store oil. Lipids stain red with Sudan III, black with osmic acid, and leave a translucent grease spot on paper.

Biological roles of lipids: long-term energy store; structural basis of membranes (phospholipids; sterols such as cholesterol in animals and phytosterols in plants — bacteria have no sterols, Mycoplasma being the exception); waterproofing (wax, cutin, suberin); insulation and cushioning in animals; hormones (steroids, and in plants gibberellins, abscisic acid and brassinosteroids); pigments (carotenoids) and vitamins A, D, E and K, which are fat-soluble.

1.2 Minerals and their biological roles

Burn a plant and the ash holds about 60 elements, but only some are essential.

Arnon and Stout (1939) gave the criteria: without the element the plant cannot complete its life cycle; no other element can replace it; and it is directly involved in the plant's metabolism.

Seventeen elements meet them — C, H and O from air and water, and 14 mineral elements from the soil.

They are grouped by the amount needed (macronutrients occur in excess of 10 mmol per kg of dry matter, micronutrients below it), not by importance.

Element (absorbed as) Main roles Deficiency sign or disease
N (NO₃⁻, NH₄⁺) amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids, chlorophyll, ATP, hormones yellowing of old leaves first; stunting
P (H₂PO₄⁻, HPO₄²⁻) ATP, nucleic acids, phospholipids, NADP dark green or purple leaves (anthocyanin); poor roots; late maturity
K (K⁺) opening and closing of stomata (guard-cell turgor); activator of over 40 enzymes; osmotic and ionic balance scorched leaf margins and tips of old leaves; weak stems (lodging)
Ca (Ca²⁺) calcium pectate of the middle lamella; spindle formation; membrane function; second messenger death of meristems and young leaf tips; blossom-end rot of tomato
Mg (Mg²⁺) centre of the chlorophyll molecule; activates RuBisCO, PEP carboxylase and the kinases; holds ribosome subunits together interveinal chlorosis of old leaves
S (SO₄²⁻) cysteine and methionine; coenzyme A, thiamine, biotin, ferredoxin chlorosis of young leaves
Fe (Fe³⁺, Fe²⁺) cytochromes, ferredoxin, catalase, peroxidase; needed to make chlorophyll though not part of it interveinal chlorosis of young leaves
Mn (Mn²⁺) splitting of water in photosystem II; activates Krebs-cycle enzymes grey speck of oats, marsh spot of pea
Zn (Zn²⁺) auxin (IAA) synthesis via tryptophan; carbonic anhydrase, alcohol dehydrogenase little leaf, rosetting; khaira disease of rice
Cu (Cu²⁺) plastocyanin; cytochrome oxidase die-back (exanthema) of citrus; reclamation disease
B (BO₃³⁻, B₄O₇²⁻) pollen germination and pollen-tube growth; Ca uptake; sugar translocation heart rot of beet, browning of cauliflower, internal cork of apple
Mo (MoO₄²⁻) nitrogenase and nitrate reductase; needed in the smallest amount of all whiptail of cauliflower
Cl (Cl⁻) with Mn, water splitting in PS II; anion balance; stomatal movement wilting, bronzing of leaves
Ni (Ni²⁺) urease; hydrogenase necrotic leaf tips (urea builds up)
Which leaves show the deficiency first?

Mobile elements (N, P, K, Mg) are moved out of old leaves to the growing parts, so the old leaves show the symptom first. Immobile elements (Ca, S, Fe, B) stay where they were deposited, so the young leaves and buds show it first.

For the macronutrients say "C. HOPKiNS CaFe, Mighty good" — C, H, O, P, K, N, S, Ca, (Fe), Mg — and remember that Fe, though it sits in the mnemonic, is a micronutrient.

Mg is in chlorophyll; Fe only helps to make it

Chlorophyll is a porphyrin ring with magnesium at its centre and four nitrogen atoms holding it; iron sits at the centre of haem (cytochromes, haemoglobin, catalase).

Iron deficiency causes chlorosis because iron is needed for chlorophyll synthesis, not because it is part of the molecule.

Mineral roles in animals and humans are asked occasionally: Fe in haemoglobin and myoglobin (lack causes anaemia); Ca and P in bones and teeth, Ca²⁺ in blood clotting and muscle contraction; Na⁺ and K⁺ in nerve impulses and osmotic balance; I in thyroxine (lack causes goitre); Co in vitamin B₁₂; Zn in carbonic anhydrase and insulin storage; F in tooth enamel.

1.3 Proteins and enzymes: structure, types and biological role

Amino acids and the peptide bond

A protein is a polymer of amino acids. Each amino acid has a central α-carbon carrying an amino group (–NH₂), a carboxyl group (–COOH), a hydrogen atom and a variable side chain (R). Twenty kinds are coded by the genetic code.

Glycine (R = H) is the simplest and the only one that is not optically active; proline is strictly an imino acid; cysteine and methionine contain sulphur; phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan are aromatic.

Plants make all twenty; humans cannot make nine essential amino acids and must eat them.

Amino acids are amphoteric. At a particular pH, the isoelectric point, the molecule carries both charges at once (–NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻) and is called a zwitterion.

The peptide bond (–CO–NH–) forms by condensation between the –COOH of one amino acid and the –NH₂ of the next. A chain of n amino acids has n − 1 peptide bonds and releases n − 1 water molecules when it forms.

The chain has a free amino end (N-terminus) and a free carboxyl end (C-terminus); the sequence is always written from N to C.

The essential amino acids

PVT TIM HaLL — Phenylalanine, Valine, Threonine, Tryptophan, Isoleucine, Methionine, Histidine, Arginine, Leucine, Lysine. Arginine is only semi-essential (needed from food in childhood), which leaves nine for adults.

The four levels of protein structure

Level What it is Bonds that hold it Example
Primary the sequence of amino acids, fixed by the gene peptide (covalent) insulin: 51 amino acids in chains A (21) and B (30), sequenced by Sanger
Secondary regular local folding: α-helix (right-handed, 3.6 residues per turn) or β-pleated sheet hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H of the backbone α-keratin of hair and wool (helix); silk fibroin (sheet)
Tertiary the whole chain folded into a compact 3-D shape H-bonds, ionic bonds, disulphide bridges (–S–S–), hydrophobic interactions myoglobin; every enzyme
Quaternary two or more folded polypeptides together the same weak bonds as tertiary haemoglobin — 2α + 2β chains, four haem groups

Pauling and Corey described the α-helix and β-sheet (1951). Only proteins with more than one polypeptide chain have a quaternary level.

Heat, extreme pH, heavy-metal ions (Hg²⁺, Pb²⁺, Ag⁺), urea and strong alcohol break the weak bonds of the secondary, tertiary and quaternary levels — the protein denatures and loses its function, but its peptide bonds (primary structure) survive.

Boiling an egg and curdling milk with lemon juice are denaturation.

Types of proteins

Basis Type Features Examples
Shape Fibrous long parallel chains; insoluble; structural keratin, collagen, fibroin, myosin, elastin
Shape Globular chains folded into a ball; soluble; functional enzymes, antibodies, haemoglobin, insulin, albumin
Composition Simple amino acids only albumins, globulins, histones, glutelins (glutenin of wheat), prolamines (zein of maize)
Composition Conjugated protein + a non-protein prosthetic group nucleoproteins, glycoproteins, lipoproteins, chromoproteins (haemoglobin, cytochromes, phytochrome), phosphoproteins (casein of milk), metalloproteins
Composition Derived made by partial hydrolysis or denaturation proteoses, peptones, peptides
Role Examples
Catalysis all enzymes — amylase, RuBisCO (the most abundant protein on Earth)
Structure collagen (the most abundant protein in mammals), keratin, extensin of plant cell walls
Transport haemoglobin, carrier proteins and channels in membranes
Defence antibodies (immunoglobulins), fibrinogen in clotting
Hormones and signalling insulin, glucagon; receptor proteins
Movement actin and myosin, tubulin, flagellin
Storage casein, ovalbumin, seed proteins (glutenin, zein)

Tests: biuret (CuSO₄ + NaOH) gives violet with two or more peptide bonds; xanthoproteic (conc. HNO₃) gives yellow with aromatic amino acids; Millon's gives red with tyrosine; ninhydrin gives purple with free amino acids.

Enzymes: nature and history

An enzyme is a biological catalyst — usually a globular protein — that speeds up a specific reaction by lowering its activation energy, without being used up and without changing the equilibrium or the energy released (\Delta G).

Year Person Contribution
1833 Payen and Persoz diastase (amylase) from malt — the first enzyme discovered
1877 Wilhelm Kühne coined the word "enzyme" ("in yeast"); some books give 1878
1894 Emil Fischer lock-and-key model
1897 Eduard Buchner a cell-free yeast extract (zymase) ferments sugar
1913 Michaelis and Menten the kinetic equation and K_m
1926 James Sumner crystallised urease from jack bean — enzymes are proteins
1958 Daniel Koshland induced-fit model
1982–83 Cech and Altman ribozymes — catalytic RNA (Nobel 1989)

Ribozymes break the rule that all enzymes are proteins: RNase P and the peptidyl transferase of the ribosome (23S rRNA in bacteria) are RNA.

Cofactors. Many enzymes need a non-protein part. The protein part alone is the apoenzyme (inactive); apoenzyme + cofactor = holoenzyme (active).

Cofactor Nature Examples
Prosthetic group organic, tightly (often covalently) bound haem in catalase and peroxidase; FAD in succinate dehydrogenase; biotin in carboxylases
Coenzyme organic, loosely bound, leaves after the reaction; most are made from B vitamins NAD⁺/NADP⁺ (niacin, B₃), FAD/FMN (riboflavin, B₂), coenzyme A (pantothenic acid, B₅), TPP (thiamine, B₁)
Metal-ion activator inorganic ion Zn²⁺ in carbonic anhydrase and carboxypeptidase; Mg²⁺ in kinases; Mo in nitrogenase; Fe and Cu in cytochrome oxidase

How enzymes work

The substrate binds to a small pocket, the active site, forming an enzyme–substrate (ES) complex; the reaction occurs and the products leave: E + S ⇌ ES → E + P. In Fischer's lock-and-key model the active site is rigid and fits the substrate exactly.

In Koshland's induced-fit model — the accepted one — the active site changes shape as the substrate binds, closing round it.

The rate rises with substrate concentration [S] and levels off when every active site is busy, at the maximum rate V_{max}. Michaelis and Menten wrote

v = \frac{V_{max}\,[S]}{K_m + [S]}

The Michaelis constant K_m is the substrate concentration at which the rate is half of V_{max}. A low K_m means high affinity — the enzyme reaches half speed at a low substrate concentration.

Useful values: at [S] = K_m, v = V_{max}/2; at [S] = 4K_m, v = 0.8\,V_{max}; at [S] = 9K_m, v = 0.9\,V_{max}.

Factors affecting enzyme activity

  • Temperature. The rate roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise (temperature coefficient Q_{10} \approx 2) up to the optimum — about 37 °C for human enzymes and 25–40 °C for most plant enzymes. Above it the enzyme denatures and the rate falls steeply, usually irreversibly. Low temperature only inactivates an enzyme, reversibly — which is why seeds and food keep in the cold. Enzymes of hot-spring bacteria survive far higher temperatures (Taq polymerase of Thermus aquaticus works at about 72 °C).
  • pH. Each enzyme has an optimum pH: pepsin about 2, salivary amylase 6.8, trypsin about 8; most cell enzymes work near 7. pH changes alter the charges on the active site.
  • Substrate concentration — a rising curve that levels off at V_{max} (Figure 1b).
  • Enzyme concentration — rate is directly proportional to [E] while substrate is in excess.
  • Inhibitors and activators — below.

Enzyme inhibition

Type Where the inhibitor binds Effect on K_m and V_{max} Reversed by more substrate? Example
Competitive active site — it resembles the substrate K_m rises, V_{max} unchanged Yes malonate blocks succinate dehydrogenase; sulpha drugs mimic PABA in bacteria; ethanol competes with methanol for alcohol dehydrogenase
Non-competitive another site on the enzyme V_{max} falls, K_m unchanged No cyanide on cytochrome oxidase; Hg²⁺, Ag⁺, Pb²⁺ on –SH groups
Irreversible binds the active site covalently enzyme destroyed for good No nerve gas (DFP) on acetylcholinesterase; penicillin on the transpeptidase of bacterial walls
Feedback (allosteric) a regulatory (allosteric) site; the inhibitor is the end product of the pathway slows the first enzyme of the pathway — isoleucine inhibits threonine deaminase; ATP inhibits phosphofructokinase

Isoenzymes (isozymes) are different molecular forms of one enzyme that catalyse the same reaction — lactate dehydrogenase has five.

Classification of enzymes

The International Union of Biochemistry (1961) sorts enzymes into six classes by the reaction they catalyse; each enzyme has an EC number whose first digit is its class. (A seventh class, translocases, was added in 2018.)

EC Class Reaction Examples
1 Oxidoreductases transfer of H or electrons (oxidation–reduction) dehydrogenases, oxidases, catalase, peroxidase
2 Transferases transfer of a group (not H) from one molecule to another transaminases (–NH₂), kinases (phosphate), e.g. hexokinase
3 Hydrolases breaking a bond with water amylase, lipase, pepsin, trypsin, sucrase, urease
4 Lyases removing a group without water, leaving a double bond (or adding to one) aldolase, fumarase, carbonic anhydrase, decarboxylases
5 Isomerases rearranging atoms within one molecule phosphohexose isomerase, triose phosphate isomerase, mutases
6 Ligases (synthetases) joining two molecules using energy from ATP DNA ligase, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase, pyruvate carboxylase
The six classes in order

"Oh The Hungry Lion Is Lazy" — Oxidoreductase, Transferase, Hydrolase, Lyase, Isomerase, Ligase (EC 1 to 6).

Classifying an enzyme you have never seen

Read the reaction, not the name. Water added across a bond that breaks → hydrolase. A group moved between two substrates → transferase. ATP spent to join two molecules → ligase. One molecule in, one rearranged molecule out → isomerase.

A molecule split without water, or a C–C bond broken to release CO₂ → lyase. H atoms or electrons moved → oxidoreductase.

Uses of enzymes: amylase in brewing and baking; pectinase to clear fruit juice; proteases and lipases in detergents; rennet (chymosin) to curdle milk for cheese; papain from papaya and bromelain from pineapple to tenderise meat; invertase for confectionery syrup; streptokinase from Streptococcus to dissolve blood clots.

Counting peptide bonds and water loss in a polypeptide

Problem. A functional plant enzyme consists of two polypeptide chains containing 120 and 80 amino acid residues respectively.

What is the total number of peptide bonds in the enzyme, and what is the molecular mass of a linear malto-oligosaccharide made of 10 glucose units (\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 = 180)?

Solution. In a linear protein of n total residues across c polypeptide chains, the number of peptide bonds is n - c: here (120 + 80) - 2 = \mathbf{198} peptide bonds.

For 10 glucose units linked by \alpha(1\rightarrow4) glycosidic bonds, 10 - 1 = 9 water molecules (9 \times 18 = 162) are lost, so M = 10 \times 180 - 162 = \mathbf{1638\text{ Da}}.

Reading a Michaelis–Menten curve at half-maximal velocity

Problem. An enzyme has V_{\max} = 60\text{ }\mu\text{mol min}^{-1} and K_m = 2.0\text{ mM}. What initial reaction velocity v_0 is obtained at [S] = 6.0\text{ mM}, and how does K_m change if a competitive inhibitor is added?

Solution. By v_0 = \frac{V_{\max}[S]}{K_m + [S]}, at [S] = 6.0\text{ mM} we have [S] = 3K_m, so v_0 = \frac{3}{4}V_{\max} = \mathbf{45\text{ }\mu\text{mol min}^{-1}}. A competitive inhibitor raises the apparent K_m while leaving V_{\max} unchanged.

Identifying mineral-deficiency mobility on the shoot

Problem. A tomato seedling grown in nutrient-deficient sand shows chlorosis first on its oldest lower leaves, whereas a second seedling shows death of the terminal bud and hooked young leaves while old leaves stay green. Which two elements are deficient?

Solution. Old-leaf chlorosis indicates a mobile element (N, P, K, or Mg) translocated to young sinks. Terminal-bud death with hooked young leaves is the signature of an immobile structural element, specifically calcium (\text{Ca}^{2+}) (or boron).

Formula and fact sheet

Item Fact

Mineral diseases khaira of rice (Zn), whiptail of cauliflower (Mo), heart rot of beet (B), grey speck of oats (Mn), die-back of citrus (Cu), blossom-end rot of tomato (Ca)
Mobile → old leaves N, P, K, Mg; immobile → young leaves: Ca, S, Fe, B
Peptide bonds n amino acids → n − 1 bonds, n − 1 H₂O
Number of possible peptides 20ⁿ for a chain of n residues

Holoenzyme apoenzyme (protein) + cofactor (prosthetic group, coenzyme or metal ion)
EC classes 1 oxidoreductase, 2 transferase, 3 hydrolase, 4 lyase, 5 isomerase, 6 ligase

Chapter summary

  • Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones; glucose is an aldohexose, fructose a ketohexose, ribulose a ketopentose.
  • Sucrose (glucose + fructose, α-1 → β-2) is non-reducing; maltose, lactose and cellobiose are reducing.
  • Starch (amylose + amylopectin) and glycogen are α-glucose stores with α-1,4 chains and α-1,6 branches; cellulose is β-1,4 glucose; chitin is β-1,4 N-acetylglucosamine; inulin is a fructose polymer.
  • A triglyceride is glycerol esterified with three fatty acids (three water molecules lost); lipids give about 39 kJ g⁻¹, more than twice carbohydrate.
  • Phospholipids are amphipathic and form membrane bilayers; steroids have four fused rings; waxes are esters of long-chain alcohols.
  • Seventeen elements are essential; Mg is in chlorophyll, Mo in nitrogenase, Mn and Cl split water, Ca forms calcium pectate, Zn is needed for auxin; mobile N, P, K, Mg show deficiency in old leaves first.
  • Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds (n − 1 for n residues); secondary structure is held by H-bonds, tertiary adds ionic, disulphide and hydrophobic bonds, quaternary needs two or more chains.
  • Enzymes lower activation energy; holoenzyme = apoenzyme + cofactor; the induced-fit model (Koshland) replaced lock-and-key (Fischer).
  • K_m is the substrate concentration at half V_{max}; competitive inhibitors raise K_m, non-competitive inhibitors lower V_{max}; feedback inhibition acts on the first enzyme of a pathway.
  • The six enzyme classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (a) — In sucrose the bond joins C-1 of glucose to C-2 of fructose, so neither unit has a free carbonyl group. Maltose, lactose and cellobiose each keep one free reducing end.

2. (c) — Cellulose is β-glucose linked β-1,4, which gives straight chains that bundle into microfibrils. Option (d) is chitin; option (b) is inulin.

3. (b) — Both have α-1,4 chains; branches start where an α-1,6 bond joins a side chain. Amylopectin branches every 24–30 units, glycogen every 8–12.

4. (d) — Inulin is a fructose polymer (fructan), unlike starch and glycogen, which are glucose polymers.

5. (c) — Chitin (β-1,4 N-acetylglucosamine), together with glucans, builds the fungal wall. Peptidoglycan is the bacterial wall polymer; cellulose the plant one.

6. (a) — Each –OH of glycerol forms an ester bond with the –COOH of a fatty acid, releasing one water molecule each — three in all. Glycosidic bonds join sugars, peptide bonds join amino acids.

7. (d) — Palmitic acid (C16:0) has no C=C double bond. Oleic (one), linoleic (two) and linolenic (three) are unsaturated.

8. (b) — Lecithin (phosphatidylcholine) is glycerol + two fatty acids + phosphate + choline, a phospholipid of membranes.

9. (a) — Chlorophyll is a porphyrin with Mg²⁺ at its centre. Iron is at the centre of haem, and is only needed for chlorophyll synthesis.

10. (c) — Molybdenum is needed in the smallest amount of all essential elements. S, Ca and Mg are macronutrients.

11. (d) — Calcium pectate cements neighbouring cells together in the middle lamella. Calcium oxalate occurs as crystals (raphides) in vacuoles, not as the cementing layer.

12. (b) — The oxygen-evolving complex of PS II contains a Mn₄CaO₅ cluster and needs Cl⁻. Copper is in plastocyanin, iron in ferredoxin and cytochromes.

13. (c) — In glycine the side chain is just H, so its α-carbon carries two identical H atoms and is not chiral. Proline is an imino acid.

14. (a) — Secondary structure (α-helix, β-sheet) is held by hydrogen bonds within the backbone. Disulphide and ionic bonds stabilise the tertiary level; peptide bonds make the primary chain.

15. (b) — Quaternary structure means two or more polypeptide chains together; haemoglobin has 2α + 2β. Iron, globular shape and O₂ transport do not define the level.

16. (d) — RuBisCO, the CO₂-fixing enzyme of the Calvin cycle, is present in huge amounts in every green leaf. Collagen is the most abundant protein of mammals only.

17. (a) — A coenzyme (NAD⁺, FAD, CoA) is a loosely bound organic cofactor. A prosthetic group is tightly bound; the apoenzyme is the protein part; holoenzyme is the complete active enzyme.

18. (c) — Koshland proposed induced fit in 1958. Fischer gave lock-and-key (1894), Sumner crystallised urease (1926), Buchner discovered zymase (1897).

19. (d) — Ligases (synthetases, EC 6) join two molecules with ATP, e.g. DNA ligase. Lyases break bonds without water or ATP.

20. (b) — Ribozymes are catalytic RNAs, such as RNase P and the peptidyl transferase rRNA of the ribosome — the exception to "all enzymes are proteins".

Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (c) — Sucrose has no free carbonyl group. Acid hydrolysis breaks the glycosidic bond and gives glucose and fructose, both reducing; neutralising lets the alkaline Benedict's test work.

2. (a) — Our amylases attack only α-1,4 links; the β-1,4 links between the glucose units of cellulose need cellulase, which humans do not make. (Lactase splits the β-1,4 bond of lactose, but that is a galactose–glucose bond.) Cellulose has no branches at all.

3. (d) — Glycogen phosphorylase removes glucose from chain ends, and heavy branching (every 8–12 units) provides many ends at once. Glycogen is α-glucose and highly branched, so(a) and(b) are false.

4. (b) — Lipid gives about 39 kJ g⁻¹ against 17 kJ g⁻¹ for starch and is stored anhydrous, so a small seed carries more energy. Lipids are not polymers and are insoluble in water.

5. (a) — Nitrogen is mobile: it is withdrawn from old leaves to feed the growing tips, so old leaves yellow first. Ca, Fe and B are immobile, so their symptoms appear in young leaves.

6. (c) — Iron is immobile and is needed for chlorophyll synthesis, so the newest leaves turn yellow between green veins. Magnesium also gives interveinal chlorosis, but in old leaves, because Mg is mobile.

7. (b) — Nitrogenase (the MoFe protein) of root-nodule bacteria reduces N₂ to NH₃; without Mo it cannot work. Leghaemoglobin and ferredoxin contain iron.

8. (d) — Heat breaks the hydrogen, ionic and hydrophobic interactions of the tertiary structure; the active site loses its shape. The peptide bonds (primary structure) survive boiling.

9. (c) — Malonate resembles succinate and occupies the active site; raising [succinate] out-competes it — the classic competitive inhibition. Non-competitive inhibition cannot be overcome by substrate.

10. (d) — With enough substrate the inhibitor is displaced, so V_{max} is still reached, but more substrate is needed for half speed: K_m rises. Option (b) describes non-competitive inhibition.

11. (a) — The biuret reaction needs two or more peptide bonds (tripeptides and larger). Option (c) is the xanthoproteic test; free amino acids and dipeptides give a negative biuret test.

12. (b) — Haemoglobin is a chromoprotein (protein + haem), a conjugated protein. Keratin is fibrous, insulin globular, and casein is a phosphoprotein, also conjugated.

1. (b) — A chain of n residues has n − 1 links, and each link releases one water molecule: 120 − 1 = 119 bonds and 119 H₂O.

2. (d) — Two peptide bonds release two water molecules: 75 + 89 + 75 − 2 × 18 = 239 − 36 = 203. Option(a) forgets the water;(b) removes only one molecule.

8. (b) — Benedict-positive means reducing (rules out sucrose); iodine-negative rules out starch; a fast cherry-red Seliwanoff's reaction marks a ketose. Glucose, an aldose, reacts only slowly and faintly.

Model answer D1: carbohydrates, lipids and proteins (10 marks)

Introduction. Biomolecules are the organic compounds that make up living matter. Carbohydrates, lipids and proteins are the major macromolecules, with nucleic acids.

Carbohydrates. Polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones with the general formula \text{C}_x(\text{H}_2\text{O})_y.

  1. Monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, ribose) are the simplest sugars and are reducing sugars. Glucose has an open-chain and a ring form (\alpha and \beta anomers).
  2. Disaccharides have two units joined by a glycosidic bond: sucrose (glucose + fructose, non-reducing), maltose (glucose + glucose) and lactose (glucose + galactose).
  3. Polysaccharides: starch (storage in plants, amylose and amylopectin), glycogen (storage in animals and fungi), cellulose (structure of the plant cell wall, \beta-1,4 links) and chitin.

Lipids. Compounds insoluble in water and soluble in organic solvents. Fats and oils are triglycerides (glycerol + 3 fatty acids). Phospholipids (with a phosphate head) form cell membranes.

Waxes (cuticle) and steroids (cholesterol) are other types. Saturated fats have no double bonds and are solid, while unsaturated ones are usually liquid.

Fats give 9\ \text{kcal g}^{-1} against 4\ \text{kcal g}^{-1} for carbohydrates and proteins.

Proteins. Polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds (CO-NH). Twenty amino acids occur.

Level Description Held by
Primary sequence of amino acids peptide bonds
Secondary \alpha-helix, \beta-sheet hydrogen bonds
Tertiary 3-D folding of one chain disulphide, ionic, hydrophobic bonds
Quaternary several chains (haemoglobin) same weak bonds

Biochemical tests.

Test Reagent Positive result for
Iodine \text{I}_2/\text{KI} starch, blue-black
Benedict's / Fehling's heat reducing sugar, brick-red precipitate
Biuret NaOH + CuSO₄ protein, violet
Sudan III stain fats, red
Ninhydrin heat amino acids, purple

Functions. Energy (glucose, fats), structure (cellulose, proteins), storage, enzymes and hormones, transport, defence and genetic information.

Numerical. A tripeptide of three amino acids has 2 peptide bonds and is formed by losing 2 molecules of water. A protein chain of 100 amino acids has 99 peptide bonds.

A diet with 300\ \text{g} of carbohydrate, 60\ \text{g} of protein and 70\ \text{g} of fat gives 4(360) + 9(70) = 2070\ \text{kcal}.

Conclusion. Carbohydrates mainly supply energy and support, lipids store energy and form membranes, and proteins do most of the structural and catalytic work.

Model answer D2: enzymes (10 marks)

Introduction. Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly globular proteins, which speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy without being used up. A few are RNA (ribozymes).

Properties.

  1. Highly specific for substrate and reaction (lock and key or induced fit).
  2. Very efficient: one catalase molecule decomposes millions of H₂O₂ molecules per minute.
  3. Work in small quantities and are not consumed.
  4. Sensitive to temperature: the optimum for human enzymes is 37^{\circ}\text{C}, and high heat denatures them.
  5. Sensitive to pH: pepsin pH 2, trypsin pH 8, salivary amylase pH 6.8.
  6. They do not alter the equilibrium, only the rate.

Mechanism. E + S ⇌ ES → E + P. The substrate binds at the active site, and in the induced-fit model the site changes shape to hold the substrate.

Michaelis-Menten equation. V = \dfrac{V_{max}[S]}{K_m + [S]}. K_m is the substrate concentration giving half the maximum velocity, and a low K_m means a high affinity.

Classification.

Class Reaction Example
Oxidoreductases oxidation-reduction dehydrogenases, catalase
Transferases group transfer transaminase
Hydrolases hydrolysis amylase, lipase, protease
Lyases non-hydrolytic removal of a group decarboxylase
Isomerases rearrangement phosphoglucose isomerase
Ligases joining using ATP DNA ligase

Cofactors. A cofactor may be a metal ion (Zn²⁺, Mg²⁺), a coenzyme (NAD⁺, FAD, derived from vitamins) or a prosthetic group (haem). The protein part without its cofactor is an apoenzyme, and the complete active enzyme is a holoenzyme.

Inhibition. Competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate and bind the active site, so K_m increases and V_{max} stays the same (malonate for succinate dehydrogenase).

Non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere, so V_{max} falls and K_m stays the same. Feedback inhibition controls metabolic pathways.

Numerical. If V_{max} = 100\ \mu\text{mol min}^{-1} and K_m = 2\ \text{mM}, then at [S] = 2\ \text{mM}, V = 50, and at [S] = 8\ \text{mM}, V = \dfrac{100\times8}{2 + 8} = 80\ \mu\text{mol min}^{-1}.

At very high [S] the rate approaches 100, as all the active sites are saturated.

Conclusion. Enzymes speed up metabolism by lowering activation energy with high specificity, and their activity is regulated by temperature, pH, inhibitors and substrate concentration.
